`RecursionError` is a built-in exception raised when the maximum recursion depth is exceeded - typically when a function keeps calling itself without reaching a base case, exhausting Python's call-stack limit. Introduced in Python 3.5, it subclasses `RuntimeError`, so older code catching `RuntimeError` for this condition still works.

`ReferenceError` is a built-in exception raised when a weak reference proxy (created with `weakref.proxy`) is used after the object it refers to has been garbage-collected. It is one of Python's rarest built-in exceptions, appearing almost exclusively in code that uses the `weakref` module for caches, observers, and other non-owning references.

`ResourceWarning` is the warning category for resource-usage problems - above all, operating-system resources like files and sockets that were opened but never explicitly closed and are being cleaned up by the garbage collector instead. It subclasses `Warning`, is ignored (hidden) by default, and is typically enabled during development via Python's development mode (`-X dev`) or a warning filter.

`RuntimeWarning` is the warning category for dubious runtime behavior - code that executes and produces a result, but in a way that suggests the programmer's mental model is wrong (a coroutine created but never awaited, a numeric operation quietly overflowing in a library). It subclasses `Warning`, is emitted via `warnings.warn()`, and is shown by default.

`self` is NOT a Python keyword. It is the CONVENTIONAL name for the first parameter of instance methods, referring to the instance the method was called on - "the object itself." The parser accepts any name; the convention is enforced by community practice (PEP 8), linters, and every tutorial ever written. Legesher translates it anyway because it appears in virtually every class body a learner reads: linguistically it is a reflexive pronoun, and most languages have strong native reflexive forms that beat any coined noun.

`StopAsyncIteration` (Python 3.5, PEP 492) is a control-flow signal, not an error: it is raised by an asynchronous iterator's `__anext__()` method to tell an `async for` loop that there are no more items. It is the async twin of `StopIteration` - same meaning, same non-error nature, delivered through the asynchronous iteration protocol.

`SyntaxError` is raised when Python's parser rejects code because it does not follow the grammar of the language - the code cannot even begin to run. The exception carries `filename`, `lineno`, `offset`, and `text` locating the problem, and since Python 3.10 its messages have become far more precise (naming unclosed brackets, suggesting missing colons or commas).

`SyntaxWarning` is the warning category for dubious syntax - source code that parses and runs, but is written in a way that usually indicates a mistake, such as testing `is` against a literal. It subclasses `Warning`, is shown by default, and is emitted at compile time (when the code is parsed), unlike its sibling `RuntimeWarning`. Its hard-failure counterpart is `SyntaxError`, where the code cannot be parsed at all.

`SystemExit` is the exception raised by `sys.exit()` to request a clean interpreter shutdown. It is a control-flow signal, not a failure: it inherits directly from `BaseException` (not `Exception`) so that ordinary `except Exception` handlers do not accidentally swallow it, and it carries the requested exit status in its `.code` attribute.

`TabError` is a subclass of `IndentationError` raised when a file's indentation mixes tab characters and spaces inconsistently - in a way whose meaning would depend on how wide a tab is displayed. Python 3 refuses to guess and rejects the code at parse time with `inconsistent use of tabs and spaces in indentation`.

`TimeoutError` is a built-in exception raised when a system function or operation times out — the allotted waiting time expires before the operation completes. It is a subclass of `OSError`, introduced by PEP 3151 in Python 3.3, and corresponds to the OS error code `ETIMEDOUT`. It has since unified Python's timeout exceptions: `socket.timeout` became an alias of it in Python 3.10, and `asyncio.TimeoutError` followed in Python 3.11, so from 3.11 onward those names all refer to this one class.

`UnboundLocalError` is a subclass of `NameError` raised when a function references a local variable before any value has been bound to it. It typically strikes when a name is assigned *somewhere* in a function - which makes it local throughout the whole function - but is read before that assignment runs. Since Python 3.11 the message spells the situation out: `cannot access local variable 'x' where it is not associated with a value`.

`UnicodeDecodeError` is a built-in exception raised when **decoding fails: converting bytes into text (bytes → str)** — for example, reading a UTF-8 file as ASCII. It is the Unicode error users hit most often, and it carries `encoding`, `object`, `start`, `end`, and `reason` attributes pinpointing exactly which bytes could not be decoded.

`UnicodeEncodeError` is a built-in exception raised when **encoding fails: converting text into bytes (str → bytes)** — for example, encoding "café" to ASCII, which has no byte for "é". It is the mirror of `UnicodeDecodeError` (the bytes → text direction) and carries `encoding`, `object`, `start`, `end`, and `reason` attributes pinpointing exactly which characters could not be encoded.

`UnicodeError` is the built-in base class for exceptions raised when Unicode encoding, decoding, or translating fails. It subclasses `ValueError`, and in practice you almost always see one of its three specific subclasses — `UnicodeDecodeError` (bytes → text failed), `UnicodeEncodeError` (text → bytes failed), or `UnicodeTranslateError` (character mapping failed) — which carry `encoding`, `object`, `start`, `end`, and `reason` attributes describing exactly what went wrong.

`UnicodeTranslateError` is a built-in exception raised when an error occurs during character translation — the `str.translate()` style of mapping characters to other characters within text (str → str), not natural-language translation and not encoding/decoding. It is the rarest member of the Unicode error family: the standard library almost never raises it, and its constructor takes `(object, start, end, reason)` with no encoding argument, since no codec is involved.

`UnicodeWarning` is the base warning category for Unicode-related concerns - suspicious comparisons, normalization surprises, or lossy text handling that works but may not do what the author intended. It subclasses `Warning`, is emitted via `warnings.warn()`, and is shown by default. In Python 3 the interpreter itself emits it only rarely; it mainly serves libraries and tools that handle text.

`UserWarning` is the default warning category: it is what `warnings.warn()` emits when no category is given. It subclasses `Warning` and marks generic warnings generated by user code (as opposed to specialized categories like `DeprecationWarning`). Like all warnings, it is advisory: it is shown by default and execution continues.

`Warning` is the base class for all warning categories in Python. It subclasses `Exception`, but unlike ordinary exceptions, warnings are advisory: they are typically emitted with `warnings.warn()` rather than raised, execution continues after they are shown, and they can be filtered, silenced, or promoted to errors via the `warnings` module and the `-W` command-line flag.

`ZeroDivisionError` is a built-in exception raised when the second argument of a division or modulo operation is zero. It applies to `/`, `//`, `%`, `divmod()`, and raising zero to a negative power — and, unlike some languages that return infinity for floats, Python raises this exception for both integer and floating-point division by zero.
